question: How is the vast distance between galaxies measured?
solution:
The correct answer is __**In light years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The vast distances between galaxies are measured in **light years** because these distances are incredibly large, and using conventional units like kilometers or miles would result in impractically large numbers.
 
• One light year is the distance that light travels in one year, which is approximately **9.46 trillion kilometers** or **5.88 trillion miles**.
 
• Light years are commonly used in astronomy to express distances between celestial objects, such as stars, galaxies, and other cosmic entities.
 
• This unit of measurement is essential for understanding the scale of the universe, as many galaxies are located millions or even billions of light years away from Earth.
 
• For example, the Andromeda Galaxy, the nearest major galaxy to the Milky Way, is located approximately **2.5 million light years** away.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Core Characteristics of Galaxies:**

 
 
• Composition: Billions to trillions of stars, stellar remnants, gas, dust, and significant dark matter, orbiting a common center of mass.
 
• Gravity: The dominant force, binding everything together, with stars orbiting the galactic core.
 
• Size & Scale: Range from dwarf galaxies (thousands of stars) to giant ellipticals (trillions of stars, millions of light-years across).
 
• Age: Most are billions of years old, some almost as old as the universe itself (around 13.8 billion years).
